newsitem.title: USA: ISSUER FOCUS - Sacramento $80 mln arena deal.
newsitem.headline: ISSUER FOCUS - Sacramento $80 mln arena deal.

text.p: The city of Sacramento, Calif., plans to come to market in two to three weeks with up to $80 million of notes to refinance a basketball arena and some of the team's debts, the city's treasurer said on Monday.

The seven-year to 10-year notes would have interest rates that reset periodically, Sacramento City Treasurer Thomas Friery said in an interview. He added that the city has yet to determine what type of interest rate hedge Sacramento would use in the transaction.
The notes, which would be issued through a city financing authority, would either be secured by municipal bond insurance or a letter of credit from a major bank, he said.
"It will be a very strong credit transaction," Friery said.
Sacramento plans to issue the notes in two to three weeks through a negotiated sale by underwriter Merrill Lynch & Co. The deal should close by April 18, Friery said.
The Sacramento City Council approved the note plan in February in a bid to keep the National Basketball Association Kings playing in the city.

With the proceeds of the note sale, the city would refinance $51.5 million of Arco Arena debt, where the Kings play. The remaining note proceeds would be used to refinance other franchise debts, Friery said.
The deal calls for the owners of the arena to pay the city the annual debt service each year.

Sacramento's general fund would be protected by more than $120 million in loan collateral, including a $20 million note secured on the Kings' franchise. The team has also signed an operating agreement to remain in Sacramento, the city said.
Sacramento officials said they do not believe the financing will affect the city's credit ratings because arena revenues should cover the debt service costs.
"We're looking for the opportunity to discuss this deal with them (the rating agencies)," Friery said.

Kings owner Jim Thomas had originally proposed a $235 million public-private partnership with the city of Sacramento to develop a sports and entertainment complex. The proposal included $90 million to retire his existing debts.
The $235 million proposal, however, came under fire, and was withdrawn by Thomas in late January. The terms of the current deal were approved by the city council on a vote of 5-to-3 on February 5.
Without a financial commitment from Sacramento, Thomas had warned he might be forced to move the team to another city.
